Phase 1 · Coach training & development

Five-minute design challenge · Size a robot lifter

Work individually with a pencil and paper. Sketch your design, calculate two values and choose a drum radius. Then compare your choice with another coach.

The problem. A servo winds a cable around a drum to raise a robot’s grabber. The cable needs to move at least 25 mm and pull with at least 2 N. For this exercise, assume the servo provides 0.060 N·m of usable torque and rotates through 120° (about 2.1 radians). Ignore friction and assume the cable winds in a single layer.

Choose a drum radius: 10, 14, 18, 24 or 32 mm.

  1. Sketch the drum, cable and direction the grabber moves.
  2. Calculate cable travel = radius × 2.1 using radius in millimetres. Calculate pull force = 0.060 ÷ radius using radius in metres.
  3. Check both requirements. Explain whether your choice gives more room for travel or more force margin. Name one thing you would test on the robot.

These are exercise values. Use the actual servo and linkage measurements when designing the competition robot.

See how the lifter works · Diagram
Trainer reveal · Compare the designs
Drum radiusCable travelPull forceResult
10 mm21 mm6.00 NTravel too short
14 mm29.4 mm4.29 NPasses with the most force margin among passing options
18 mm37.8 mm3.33 NPasses with room in both requirements
24 mm50.4 mm2.50 NPasses with the most travel among passing options
32 mm67.2 mm1.88 NPull force too low

Invite coaches who chose different radii to defend their choices. A larger radius moves more cable for the same servo angle and gives less pull force for the same torque. Ask how friction, battery condition and clearance would affect the bench test. Then apply the same reasoning to the robot’s lifter and grabber.

Challenge, missions and rules

Start with the official field and mission descriptions. For each mission, identify the game object, its starting condition, the allowed robot contact, and what the judge must see at the end. Check the scoring conditions and any layout changes before choosing a mechanism.

Robot design checks. Start within 20 × 20 × 20 cm and 1 kg. Use a Quarky-series main controller and program in PictoBlox. Check power limits, inspection requirements, category control rules and allowed expansion before committing to a design. Measure the physical robot in its legal starting pose. CAD views may show mechanisms extended.

Plan the robot’s path and mission actions
  1. Mark the home point, mission targets, clearance around field elements and any positions that change between rounds.
  2. For each mission, draw the route from the start pose to the approach pose, the mechanism action, and the exit pose for the next mission.
  3. Mark where the robot can use line following, timed drive or AprilTag detection. Include a recovery action and test whether the robot can still complete the next task.
  4. Break the scoring action into Push, Pull, Pick or Place. A single mission may need several. Identify what the robot has to sense before each action.

Discuss on screen. Ask each coach to name one action, the direction of force or travel, and the evidence that shows it worked.

Select the servo mechanism · Push, pull, pick and place
ActionMechanisms to compareWhat to test before selecting
PushServo flap, pivoting arm or short linkage.Contact height, direction, reach, force and room to retract.
PullServo hook or grabber with a linkage. Rack and pinion when the pull needs guided straight travel.Positive engagement, release at the end, useful stroke and resistance to binding.
PickServo grabber with geared jaws or a parallel linkage. A lifter can raise the object after gripping.Jaw opening, approach tolerance, grip under motion and room for the servo to close without stalling.
PlaceServo lifter or four-bar for controlled height and orientation. Rack and pinion for guided linear travel.Required height and stroke, object orientation, drop accuracy and clearance to withdraw.

A simple linkage redirects servo rotation. A parallelogram four-bar can keep the tool orientation nearly constant through its travel. A rack and pinion turns rotation into linear movement and needs a guide to keep the rack engaged. Compare motion, repeatability, starting size, weight, servo load and reuse across missions. Choose the simplest mechanism that reliably achieves the legal scoring action and fits the robot.

Coach decision. Pick two mechanisms for one mission, test them from the same approach, then explain which you would build and why.

Two-day agenda

Follow the sequence at the group’s pace. Each day is capped at seven hours including breaks. Task durations are tentative and may vary with build and testing progress.

Day 1 · Discuss, assemble, and program
SequenceActivity
DiscussionStart with the five-minute lifter calculation. Compare designs, then discuss the field and reveal the reference robot during mechanism selection.
Build and wireAssembly and coding setup, part 1. Allow about three hours across both setup blocks. Build the drivetrain and mount Quarky, Intellio, grabber, lifter, and flap. Connect and label motors and servo ports. Inspect and log both boards’ battery status.
LunchLunch
Setup and calibrationAssembly and coding setup, part 2. Open the actual PictoBlox project, verify connection, drive direction, servo home and travel, camera and tag IDs. Calibrate left and right IR sensors on the mat. Save the working baseline. Rotate hands-on roles throughout.
Program and bench-testTrace the match program. Bench-test each servo routine, timed moves, swing and point turns, and line following. Then test tag reads and the decision made on a valid or missed read.
BreakBreak

Daily conclusionConclusion, about 10 minutes. Each coach names one thing they can now teach. Confirm Day 2 starts with a cold start and C1/C6 testing.

SequenceActivity
Cold start and tuningCold start, code and tune C1 and C6 across official layouts. Test each recognition decision, approaches, servo timing and recovery from missed reads. Link C1–C6 and the bonus.
LunchLunch

BreakBreak

Daily conclusionConclusion and feedback, about 10 minutes. Commit to the first student session, record readiness and request ideas for future competition trainings.

Robot assembly guide

Quarky Robot Final-1.step
Exploded view · Quarky Robot Final-1
Mounts and connection plateDrive motors and wheelsFront uplift linksFront grabber partsRear geared arms and mountGeekservosQuarky board
Assembled robot · 360° rotation
Step 1 · Chassis and drive

Identify the front of the robot. Fit the two DC motors, wheels and chassis supports using the reference build. Check that each wheel rotates freely. Label the motor leads DRIVE_LEFT and DRIVE_RIGHT from the robot’s forward-facing perspective.

Step 2 · Lifter and grabber

Use the teal Front Uplift links and connectors and the violet front grabber components as shown. Match their pivot and mounting orientation to the assembled CAD and reference robot. Fit the lifter and grabber mechanically, with each servo linkage disconnected for initial calibration. Support the lifter and check travel by moving the detached mechanisms gently by hand. Check clearance in both the raised and lowered positions.

Step 3 · Flap

Compare the pink rear geared arms and centre mount in the CAD with the flap fitted to your reference robot. Confirm the flap’s mounting and motion on the physical build. With the servo linkage detached, confirm the flap clears the chassis, wheels, grabber and lifter throughout its travel.

Step 4 · Quarky, Intellio and wiring

With power off, mount the boards and battery, align Quarky’s IR sensors toward the mat, and aim the Intellio camera at the expected tag height. Match the two motor leads and three servo leads to the actual wiring map. Label each servo by mechanism and record its board and port. Secure cables away from wheels and moving linkages.

Step 5 · Calibrate and commission

Test motor direction with the wheels lifted. Centre each unloaded servo using the verified range for its model. Power off before fitting the horn and linkage. Test the mechanism in small steps and record safe home and travel limits. On the mat, calibrate both IR sensors, verify a live AprilTag read, and run one scoring action at low speed.

Intellio AprilTag guide

Intellio Vision extensionAprilTag camera setupPrintable AprilTags (PDF)
Step 1 · Connect and choose the correct PictoBlox mode

Open a copy of the working robot project and record its mode. For onboard detection, select Quarky Intellio in Block Coding, switch to Upload Mode, and add AprilTags Intellio Vision. Verify compatible PictoBlox and Intellio firmware before the session. For a Stage Mode project, use PictoBlox’s separate universal AprilTag extension and follow the camera feed used by the working project.

Step 2 · Initialise the camera and tag family

At startup, use Initialise AprilTag and Camera Resolution. Match the family to the printed field tag. Intellio Vision supports 16h5, 25h9 and 36h11. Bench-test 160 × 120 first for a faster read, and compare 240 × 240 if distant tags are unclear. Keep the full border in view and avoid glare. Enter the measured tag side length using the block’s units if using distance or pose.

Step 3 · Read a fresh frame and choose an action

At the scan point, slow or stop the drive. Run Analyse Image from Intellio Onboard Camera, then check the count and expected ID from that frame. Match the detected numeric ID to a table of mission, scan position and next action. Try a short, bounded rescan when the expected ID is missing. If the read still fails, stop or follow the route’s tested fallback. Clear the previous decision at the start of each scan.

Bench test first. Show a known tag, an unexpected tag and an empty frame. Confirm that only a valid detection triggers the planned action. Then trace how the vision result reaches the drive or servo routine in the actual project.

Step 4 · Field test and troubleshoot
  • Zero detections: Confirm mode, extension, firmware, tag family, lighting and camera view. Check that image analysis runs before the ID read.
  • Wrong action: Compare the live numeric ID and route mapping. Confirm the code uses the latest frame and handles other tags in view.
  • Bench pass, field miss: Recheck the actual approach distance and angle, motion blur and whether the lifter or flap blocks the camera.

Repeat on the official field layouts used in the relevant missions. Follow the event’s camera setup for each mission, including any designated field webcam. STEMpedia Intellio Vision reference

Quarky specifications · Intellio specifications

Geekservo · Position, safe travel and mechanism setup

A positional servo uses internal feedback to move its shaft toward a commanded angle. The PictoBlox angle is the target. To find the actual position on our setup, observe the horn against a reference mark or protractor. Use a separate feedback signal only if the exact servo and wiring support it.

  1. Power off, support the mechanism and disconnect its linkage from the servo horn. Identify the servo model and confirm it is positional, its supported command range, and the signal, power and ground pins.
  2. With the unloaded shaft free to move, command the model’s documented neutral and use a light pointer to confirm movement. STEMpedia uses 90° for its documented 180° servo. Confirm the Geekservo model before using that value or changing the pulse range.
  3. With power off, fit the horn so the linkage starts in a clear, usable position. Power up and move in small steps. Stop at buzzing, stalling, binding or unwanted contact. Back away from the limit and leave clearance before recording the safe operating range. Keep fingers clear of linkages.
  4. Record GRABBER_OPEN, GRABBER_CLOSED, LIFTER_UP, LIFTER_DOWN, and the flap’s two working positions. Also record each home position and safe minimum and maximum. Clamp commands to those limits in the shared servo routines.

Coach drill. Demonstrate the commanded angle and observed horn position, then show why one safe servo angle may still be unsafe with the linkage attached.

STEMpedia servo calibration guide

DC motors · Motor names, swing turns and point turns

The geared DC motors drive the wheels continuously. The driver controls direction and power. PWM percentage is a command, and the actual speed depends on the load and battery. There are no drive encoders on this robot.

Define left and right from the robot’s forward-facing view. Label leads and code DRIVE_LEFT and DRIVE_RIGHT. Record the physical port and forward setting for each. With wheels clear of the mat, command each side separately at low power. Confirm both drive the robot forward when given forward commands. Test straight on the mat, then adjust trim if it drifts.

ActionLeft wheelRight wheel
ForwardForwardForward
ReverseReverseReverse
Swing leftStopForward
Swing rightForwardStop
Point leftReverseForward
Point rightForwardReverse

A swing turn pivots near the stationary wheel. A point turn counter-rotates around the robot’s centre when wheel speeds are matched. Test both for clearance with the actual mechanism positions.

Timed motion exercise. Build a PictoBlox block that sets both motor commands, waits for a duration in seconds, and then stops both. Use a marked start pose to tune a short straight move, a swing and a point turn. Run each three times and record power on both sides, seconds, observed distance or angle, load and battery state. Recheck after a battery change and use a line or tag to re-establish position where the route permits.

Quarky motion · Motor direction and trim

IR sensors · Calibration and line following
  1. Mount both onboard IR sensors facing the mat. Check that the sensors are clean, level and unobstructed. Record the installed height and spacing, and confirm which input is IR_LEFT and which is IR_RIGHT.
  2. Read each sensor over the actual black line and white background at operating height and lighting. Take several samples per surface. If the black and white ranges are clearly separated, start with a threshold between those ranges for each sensor. If the ranges overlap, fix the mounting or lighting and sample again.
  3. Set the two thresholds in PictoBlox and observe each sensor on black and white to verify its reported state. The Quarky Advanced Line Following calibration block is an alternative. Make sure the sensors cross both surfaces during its calibration motion.
  4. At low speed, move the robot from its centred pose toward each edge and observe the two sensor states. Program the correction that steers it back. Verify the response for all four combinations on the actual mat. Depending on sensor spacing and line width, matching states can indicate a centred pose, a junction or a lost line. Use the expected route and recent readings to distinguish them, and stop if a short recovery times out.

Coach drill. Show the live left and right readings, explain the chosen thresholds, then complete three clean line-follow runs from the same start and a deliberate line-loss test.

Quarky IR sensors · PictoBlox IR calibration block

Battery maintenance · Pre-run checklist
  • Before practice: Label and charge the approved packs using the manufacturer’s charging method. Inspect the packs, connectors and leads. Keep a charged spare ready and record which pack is installed.
  • During testing: Watch for slower drive, incomplete servo travel, resets or wireless interruptions under load. Check battery status and connections before changing code. Compare runs at similar charge levels and recheck the straight move and turn after a pack swap.
  • After practice: Power off, follow the manufacturer’s storage instructions and note packs that behave inconsistently. Stop using swollen, damaged, leaking or unusually hot packs. Charge on a firm surface away from flammable materials using approved equipment.

Coach development and readiness

Individual readiness check
  • Can commission the robot from power-off and verify the three mechanisms and camera.
  • Can trace one AprilTag decision and diagnose a fault without trainer prompts.
  • Can demonstrate and teach a legal scoring action, then explain how the group completed all six missions and the bonus.
  • Can guide a student project entry and name the first hands-on activity for their assigned team.
Closing feedback prompts
  1. Rate your confidence leading your assigned team before and after this training, from 1 to 5. What accounts for the change?
  2. What can you now teach independently? Where would you still want support?
  3. Which practical block should we keep or improve?
  4. Which competition or technical topic should the next training cover, and what would you like to build or practise?

30 hours of skill building · Suggested allocation
  • 4 h · Game rules, scoring, ethics and mission planning
  • 6 h · Robot assembly, wiring and three mechanism tests
  • 7 h · PictoBlox, drive control, reusable routines and debugging
  • 5 h · AprilTag recognition, decision logic and missed reads
  • 6 h · Mission integration, field tests and engineering iteration
  • 2 h · Student demonstration, project entries and readiness check

By hour 30 students should be able to explain a design choice, build and troubleshoot a mechanism, modify code, show a legal scoring action and back up an improvement with test evidence.

After hour 30: Each assigned coach leads team practice, chooses the route and mission priorities with students, and adjusts strategy from timed match results.

Match rules and scoring reminders
  • Elementary has 4 minutes and may use manual or autonomous control subject to the mode-switch rules. Junior and Senior have 3 minutes and run fully autonomously.
  • Quarky or Quarky Intellio is the main controller. Program with PictoBlox. Initial size limit is 20 × 20 × 20 cm and maximum mass is 1 kg.
  • Challenge 1 uses a coin toss and Challenge 6 uses a dice roll to determine the starting arrangements. The timer starts on the judge’s signal and continues during the run.
  • Use the required recognition where applicable. The official score sheet deducts 10 points per foul. Use the official mission requirements to judge finish states, partial credit, and bonus eligibility.
